body.p_39: On the project's test setups, HYBRID's alt-az EKF tracking came within about a factor of two of equatorial guiding with PHD2, on a mount geometry that is harder to track. Independent comparisons on the same equipment and under the same conditions would be needed to confirm these results.

article.headline: Design Goals and Architecture of a Self-Guiding Observatory
article.deck: How the voice-controlled telescope system and its predictive tracking work: the three tracking layers, the ASCOM and MCP interfaces, the role of voice control, and the current roadmap.

sidebar.stat_desc: Kalman filter for reactive correction, Extended Kalman for nonlinear dynamics, ML layer for predictive adaptation.

body.p_1: Passive sidereal tracking, active Kalman/EKF correction from plate solves, and ML-based tuning of the filter's noise parameters.
body.p_2: Many settings in a telescope control session are changed by hand at the computer: exposure time, target, filter, focus. At low temperatures, with gloves on and dew forming on the optics, each of these changes takes time and interrupts the session, and conditions such as seeing can change in the meantime. Reducing these manual interventions is one of the design goals of HYBRID Telescope Control.
body.p_3: Most telescope control follows a command-and-response model. The user, or a sequence the user has written, tells the mount where to point and the camera when to expose. Drift and focus shifts are detected by measurement — autoguiding, periodic autofocus — and corrected after they occur. Established sequencers automate much of this. For long-exposure astrophotography, where a single exposure can last 10 minutes and a session 8 hours, the approach works, but each correction follows the error it responds to.
body.p_4: Consider tracking accuracy. A telescope mount, even a good equatorial mount, drifts. Periodic error from the worm gear, flexure from temperature changes, atmospheric refraction, wind loading and polar alignment error all contribute to drift that degrades image quality. The standard solution is autoguiding: a second camera watches a guide star and sends correction pulses to the mount. This works well. In its basic form it is reactive — the guide star must drift before a correction is applied — although some guiding algorithms add prediction of periodic error.
body.p_5: Guide star drifts → Camera detects error → Software computes correction → Pulse sent to mount → Mount corrects. Latency: 1-3 seconds. Error accumulates between corrections.
body.p_6: Plate solve measures position → Kalman filter predicts drift → ML layer adapts noise parameters → Correction includes predicted drift → Mount follows the target. Measurement cycle: about 5 seconds. Accuracy depends on how well the model predicts the drift.
body.p_7: The design assumes that no single tracking algorithm covers all conditions. Atmospheric conditions change, mechanical properties shift with temperature, and different mount geometries require different mathematical models. HYBRID therefore uses a three-layer architecture that combines passive, active and predictive tracking:
body.p_8: The architecture was revised during field testing. The Kalman filter's matrix dimensions were corrected, the EKF correction pathway was completed, and the ML training pipeline was extended from single-axis to dual-axis regression. Each change followed a specific failure or limitation found in testing.
body.p_9: HYBRID does not implement its own hardware protocols. It builds on the ASCOM Platform, the widely used standard for amateur telescope control on Windows. ASCOM provides a unified API for mount control, camera operations, focuser positioning, filter wheel selection and observatory automation. HYBRID's ASCOM controller wrapper (1,080 lines of C#) handles GOTO, slew, park, tracking and pulse-guide operations, including error handling and state management.
body.p_10: ASCOM defines how software talks to hardware; it does not define how an AI assistant discovers and calls telescope functions. For that, HYBRID uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It exposes 47 telescope tools through an MCP server, making them available to any MCP-compatible AI assistant. Claude Desktop can discover these tools, read their parameters, and chain them into multi-step sequences. The AI assistant handles the orchestration, and ASCOM handles the hardware.
body.p_11: Voice control is intended to reduce manual interaction during the observing workflow. Typical scenarios:
body.p_12: The Kalman filter predicts mount drift. The ML layer adapts to changing conditions. The scheduler selects targets based on altitude, weather and session history. Decisions within a session are based on the system's own state estimates rather than manual input.
body.p_13: ASCOM commands translate predictions into motion. The mount slews to targets. The camera captures exposures. The focuser maintains focus as the temperature drops. The filter wheel selects the filter for each target. The meridian flip is executed and then verified.
body.p_14: When clouds arrive, the scheduler pauses and waits. When the seeing improves, the ML layer tightens the noise parameters. When a target sets below the horizon limit, the system moves to the next target. When the session ends, the telescope parks and the system shuts down.
body.p_15: Each of these components is implemented in the current version: the Kalman filter, the ML layer, the scheduler, the voice pipeline and the ASCOM interface. The remaining work is integration — making them operate together reliably in real observatory conditions, with falling temperatures, passing clouds, and equipment running unattended through the night.
body.p_16: The development roadmap reflects the progression from voice control to autonomous operation:
body.p_17: HYBRID Telescope Control is MIT-licensed and open to contribution. The source code is available for inspection, modification and redistribution. Open source lets users read the code that makes decisions for unattended equipment, such as a mount running through the night.
body.p_18: The design draws on more than 20 open-source projects: NINA's sequencer architecture, PHD2's guiding algorithms, Stellarium's sky chart rendering, Siril's image stacking, the OnStep community's hardware interface standards, and the MCP ecosystem's tool protocol. HYBRID is released under the MIT license so that its own code is available to others in the same way.
body.p_19: A second goal is to accept complete instructions in natural language. A wake-word assistant can map a phrase such as "go to M31" to a single command. HYBRID is designed to handle a multi-step request such as "slew to M31, plate solve, center it, autofocus, and start imaging for two hours with 180-second exposures": it runs the steps in order, handles errors, and adapts to conditions with limited human intervention.
body.p_20: HYBRID adds predictive tracking. The Kalman filter, a standard estimation method in navigation and control, estimates the mount's drift state from plate-solve measurements and projects it forward in time. Each correction therefore includes the drift expected before the next measurement, not only the error already observed.
body.p_21: Cold-weather operation. At -5°C, removing gloves to operate a laptop is uncomfortable and slows work down. Voice control allows changing targets, adjusting exposures and starting imaging sequences without using the keyboard.
body.p_22: Multi-tasking. While the telescope is imaging one target, you can queue the next target by voice, check the weather forecast, or adjust the scheduler — without interrupting the current imaging session.
body.p_23: Accessibility. Voice input offers an alternative to mouse and keyboard for observers with limited mobility. At public outreach events, it allows telescope control to be demonstrated by speaking.
body.p_24: Multi-step sequences. Commands can be chained. "Slew to M81, plate solve, autofocus, and start imaging for 30 minutes with 180-second exposures" is a single utterance that triggers four MCP tool calls, each dispatched to the ASCOM API. The AI assistant handles the sequence logic; the hardware handles the motion.
body.p_25: The longer-term design goal is autonomous operation: an observatory that carries out the following functions without manual input:

article.headline: Kalman to OnStep: How a Tracking Correction Reaches the Mount
article.deck: The five-step path from the Kalman state vector to an OnStep rate command, shown with the Python and ASCOM code involved and the timing of each step.

sidebar.stat_desc: Approximate time for one command to travel from Python to OnStep over ASCOM Alpaca. The three requests of a correction cycle take about 150 ms in total; the plate solve (about 2 s) takes most of the cycle time.

body.h2_2: Step 1: Plate Solve — Measuring the Real Error
body.h2_4: Step 3: Python Converts to OnStep Commands
body.h2_5: Step 4: ASCOM Alpaca — The HTTP Bridge
body.h3_5: Method B: Custom Rates — Drift Compensation
body.p_1: Every five to fifteen seconds, the HYBRID Telescope Control system runs the following sequence: a camera captures a star field, a plate solver determines the exact pointing position, a Kalman filter predicts future drift, Python converts those predictions into OnStep commands, ASCOM Alpaca transmits them over HTTP, and the mount firmware adjusts its tracking rate — all before the next image exposure begins. This article traces the complete communication path with the code involved.
body.p_2: The code shows that the Kalman filter never communicates directly with OnStep. It performs pure mathematical computation in Python memory — updating state vectors, predicting future drift, and computing optimal tracking rates. A separate layer of Python code then translates those predictions into two distinct types of commands that are transmitted via ASCOM Alpaca's HTTP REST interface. This separation is the key to understanding how the pipeline is structured and how the measured ±0.5 arcsecond result is obtained.
body.p_3: Every tracking cycle follows the same five-stage pipeline. The stages execute sequentially within a single loop iteration, and the entire sequence repeats every 5 to 15 seconds depending on the exposure time and plate-solve latency. Here is the flow at a glance:
body.p_4: The cycle begins with a camera exposure. The guide camera captures a 1-second image of the star field currently in the telescope's field of view. This image is handed to ASTAP, which performs plate-solving: matching the observed star patterns against its catalog to determine the Right Ascension and Declination the telescope is actually pointing at — the measured position, as opposed to the position the mount reports.
body.p_5: The plate-solve output produces two values: the solved coordinates (actual RA and Dec) and the measured error (the difference between the target position and the actual position, converted to arcseconds). This error is the input to every subsequent step.
body.p_6: At this stage, the system has a measured error in arcseconds. The telescope is off by -0.45 arcsec in Right Ascension and +0.32 arcsec in Declination. These numbers are passed directly to the Kalman filter.
body.p_7: This stage involves no communication at all. The Kalman filter runs entirely in Python memory. It does not open sockets, does not send HTTP requests, does not touch ASCOM. It is a pure mathematical function: given a measurement error and a time delta, update the internal state and compute the optimal tracking rate.
body.p_8: The state vector is four elements: RA position error, RA velocity (drift rate), Dec position error, and Dec velocity. On each cycle, three operations execute in sequence — update, predict, and compute optimal rate.
body.p_9: The update step fuses the new measurement with the filter's prior prediction. The Kalman gain matrix K determines how much weight to give the new measurement versus the existing state estimate. A high-confidence measurement pulls the state toward the observed error; a noisy measurement is trusted less.
body.p_10: The predict step projects the current state forward in time using the velocity estimates. If RA is drifting at -0.09 arcsec/sec, in 5 seconds the error grows to -0.45 + (-0.09 × 5) = -0.9 arcsec. This prediction is the main difference from a simple proportional correction: it estimates where the error is going, not just where it is.
body.p_11: The optimal rate combines three factors: the base sidereal rate, the Kalman-predicted drift compensation, and a proportional correction based on the current error. The correction gain parameter (0.5 = 50%) controls how aggressively the system responds — higher values correct faster but risk oscillation.
body.p_12: Next, the result is translated into commands. The Kalman filter has computed an optimal tracking rate — a single number in arcsec/sec. Python must convert this into two distinct types of commands that OnStep understands. These are not alternatives; both are sent every cycle, in a specific order.
body.p_13: The SYNC command is a standard ASCOM operation. It does not use Kalman predictions at all — it simply tells OnStep the real coordinates. OnStep then recalculates its pointing model, correcting systematic errors like polar alignment drift.
body.p_14: Every command from Python reaches OnStep through ASCOM Alpaca's HTTP REST interface. Python has no serial or USB link to OnStep; it sends standard HTTP PUT requests to a local network endpoint, and the ASCOM server handles the serial connection. As a result, the control software can run on any machine on the network.
body.p_15: The ASCOM Alpaca server runs on the computer connected to OnStep, listening on port 11111. Python sends a PUT request with the command string in the body. ASCOM translates the LX200 protocol command to serial, sends it to OnStep's USB interface, receives the response, and returns it to Python as a JSON object.
body.p_16: The entire HTTP round-trip completes in approximately 50 milliseconds. Two additional PUT requests follow — one for the Dec offset, one for the SYNC coordinates — bringing the total ASCOM communication time to roughly 150 milliseconds for a complete correction cycle.
body.p_17: OnStep maintains these adjusted rates until the next correction arrives. Between plate-solve cycles, the telescope drifts at the corrected rate — which is why the Kalman prediction matters. A simple proportional correction would fix the current error but leave the drift uncompensated. Kalman's prediction of where the error will be in 5 seconds allows OnStep to track at a rate that compensates the predicted drift during the interval between corrections.
body.p_18: The timeline below shows an example tracking cycle, with timestamps for each step:
body.p_19: In this example, the first cycle measured -0.45 arcsec RA error. After 5 seconds with the Kalman corrections applied, the next cycle measured -0.05 arcsec, a reduction of about 90% over one cycle. With SYNC and CUSTOM RATES both active, the steady-state error on the test setup settles at approximately ±0.5 arcseconds.
body.p_20: A common question about this architecture is: why use two methods instead of one? The answer lies in what each method corrects. SYNC fixes the current position. CUSTOM RATES fixes the rate of drift. They solve different problems, and both are needed.
body.p_21: Consider what happens if only SYNC is used, without custom rates. The position is corrected to zero error, but the mount continues tracking at the standard sidereal rate. Over the next 5 seconds, the same systematic drift that caused the original error rebuilds. By the next plate solve, the error has grown back to nearly the same value. SYNC alone only reacts, and has to correct the same error again in every cycle.
body.p_22: Now consider custom rates without SYNC. The Kalman filter predicts drift and adjusts the tracking rate accordingly, but the initial position offset is never corrected. The mount tracks at a slightly different speed, but from the wrong starting point. The error decreases more slowly.
body.p_23: Used together in the correct order — SYNC first to establish the correct position, then CUSTOM RATES to maintain it — the two methods form a closed feedback loop. SYNC resets the error to zero. Custom rates limit how much it grows. On the test setup, the result is a steady-state tracking error of approximately ±0.5 arcseconds, maintained over imaging sessions of several hours.
body.p_24: The system uses a specific set of OnStep LX200 protocol commands, each serving a distinct purpose in the correction pipeline:
body.p_25: When the Kalman filter is not available — for example, during initial startup before enough plate-solve measurements have accumulated, or if the kalman_filter module fails to import — the system falls back to a simpler method. In these cases, a proportional correction replaces Kalman's predictions:
body.p_26: The proportional fallback still sends both SYNC and CUSTOM RATES — the two-method approach is maintained regardless of whether Kalman is active. The difference is that the fallback reacts to the current error only, without predicting future drift. This yields roughly ±2 arcsecond precision compared to Kalman's ±0.5 arcsecond.
body.p_27: The filter is a pure mathematical function. It receives measurements and returns predictions. The translation to hardware commands happens in a separate Python layer.
body.p_28: SYNC corrects position. Custom rates correct drift. Both execute every cycle, always in the same order: SYNC first, then rates. The order matters — rates must be applied to the correct position.
body.p_29: Every command travels as an HTTP PUT request to a local network endpoint. No proprietary protocol is involved, and Python has no direct hardware link. The ASCOM server translates HTTP to serial LX200 protocol for OnStep.
body.p_30: Plate solve: 2 seconds. Kalman computation: 1 millisecond. Three HTTP requests: 150 milliseconds. OnStep application: instantaneous. Total correction time: approximately 2.2 seconds within a 5-second cycle.
body.p_31: If Kalman is unavailable, the system falls back to proportional correction. If ASCOM is unreachable, the tracking loop continues with sidereal-only tracking. In both cases the mount keeps tracking.
body.p_32:
ascom.sync_to_coordinates(ra, dec)

Tells OnStep: "You are at this position NOW." Corrects the position error. Realigns the pointing model. Instantaneous effect — fixes where the telescope thinks it is.
body.p_33:
ascom.command_string(":SXTR,offset#")

Tells OnStep: "Track at THIS speed." Compensates predicted drift. Continuous effect — adjusts how fast the telescope moves between plate solves.
body.p_34: At this point the Kalman predictions become motor commands. The :SXTR and :SXTD commands are OnStep-specific — they set RA and Dec tracking rate offsets relative to sidereal. A +0.068 arcsec/sec offset means OnStep tracks 0.068 arcsec/sec faster than sidereal, compensating the drift that Kalman predicted.
body.p_35: OnStep receives the LX200 protocol commands and applies them immediately to its tracking motor controller. The :SXTR command modifies the RA tracking rate by adding the specified offset to the base sidereal rate. The :SXTD command does the same for Declination.
body.p_36: The recommended commands are :SXTR and :SXTD (offsets) rather than :SX9A/:SX9B (absolute rates). Offset commands are additive — they adjust relative to the current rate — which means OnStep's own sidereal tracking remains active as the baseline. Absolute rate commands would override the sidereal baseline entirely, which can cause issues if the correction is momentarily interrupted.

article.headline: The ML + Kalman Hybrid: Adding a Predictive Layer
article.deck: The Kalman filter corrects measured drift; the ML layer predicts recurring residual errors. This article describes how the two are combined — 24 input features, SDCA regression, a confidence gate and a fusion gain — and where the approach has limits.

sidebar.stat_desc: Position, temporal, environmental, and statistical features extracted from each plate-solve cycle feed the prediction model.

body.h2_1: The Fundamental Principle: From Estimation to Contextual Prediction
body.h2_3: How It Works: The Control Loop
body.h2_4: The Concrete Example: Gear Oscillation at Dec 45°
body.h2_5: Fusion Formula: The Mathematics of Combination
body.h3_1: Layer 1: The Reflex System — Kalman Filter
body.h3_2: Layer 2: The Cognitive System — ML Predictive Model
body.h3_3: Step 1: Data Collection — Building the Learning Base
body.h3_4: Step 2: Model Training — SDCA Regression with Confidence Gate
body.h3_5: Step 3: Real-Time Integration — The Fusion Loop
body.p_1: The Kalman filter is a generalist model. It relies on simple physical equations — a constant-velocity model that assumes drift follows predictable, linear patterns. It is optimal for estimating the current state and the immediately future state, but it cannot learn or adapt to complex, recurring patterns specific to your mount, its position in the sky, or the ambient environmental conditions.
body.p_2: Machine learning, by contrast, can find such patterns in historical data. An LSTM network can learn that "every time the telescope reaches Dec 45°, a gear oscillation occurs every 5 minutes" — a pattern that the constant-velocity model does not represent. The aim of the hybrid design is to combine the two so that each approach covers part of the other's limitations.
body.p_3: The Kalman filter provides the foundation — real-time, mathematically grounded drift estimation with known convergence properties. The ML layer builds on top of that foundation, learning mount-specific mechanical patterns from hundreds of hours of guiding data. The combination is intended to correct both linear drift and recurring mount-specific errors.
body.p_4: The hybrid system operates on two distinct layers that run simultaneously, each handling a different timescale and a different class of tracking error.
body.p_5: The low-level Kalman filter continues to function exactly as before. Its role is to provide a smoothed, real-time estimate of the current drift — both position and velocity — by filtering measurement noise from plate-solve data. On equatorial mounts, a 4-state model (RA position, RA velocity, Dec position, Dec velocity) captures the essential linear dynamics. On Alt-Az mounts, a 6-state Extended Kalman filter handles the nonlinear coordinate transformation.
body.p_6: This layer operates on a ~5-second cadence, responding to each plate-solve measurement. It is the system's fast reflex: it runs continuously and, under its linear-Gaussian assumptions, gives the optimal estimate for the linear portion of the drift.
body.p_7: The high-level ML layer analyzes the Kalman filter's outputs over a longer time window — from several minutes to tens of minutes — along with contextual data about the mount state, environment, and correction history. Its purpose is to predict a more complex, future drift error that the Kalman filter's simple physics model cannot represent.
body.p_8: This layer is predictive: it aims to anticipate recurring errors before they appear in the measurements. It learns that certain combinations of time, temperature, and telescope orientation produce specific mechanical behaviors, and it prepares corrections in advance rather than reacting after the fact.
body.p_9: For the ML model to function, it needs a database of contextual snapshots. At every guiding cycle — approximately every 5 seconds — the system records a snapshot containing 24 input features organized into four categories:
body.p_10: The prediction target — the label — is the future residual error. Specifically: "What will the guide sensor measure as drift in 60 seconds, despite the Kalman filter's standard corrections?" Once this future value is known, it becomes ground truth for training the model.
body.p_11: The model uses Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent (SDCA) regression, an optimization method for regularized linear models. Training happens offline on hundreds of hours of recorded guiding data, where the model learns to associate contextual features with future drift error.
body.p_12: An important design choice is the R² confidence gate. The ML model is only deployed if it demonstrates sufficient predictive power on unseen data. If the model's R² falls below a defined threshold — indicating it has not learned reliable patterns — the system falls back to Kalman-only tracking. This prevents an untrained or poorly trained model from injecting noise into the control loop.
body.p_13: Once trained and deployed, the ML model operates in parallel with the Kalman filter during live guiding:
body.p_14: Consider an illustrative scenario. A mount has a specific gear mesh pattern that causes a small oscillation every 5 minutes when the telescope is at a particular Declination.
body.p_15: The ML model predicts mechanical errors 60 seconds before they appear, giving the control loop time to prepare a correction that reduces the disturbance.
body.p_16: The fusion formula is simple. It is the point where the reactive Kalman correction and the predictive ML correction are combined into one command.
body.p_17: C_K and C_ML operate on different timescales. C_K corrects what has already happened — the current drift error measured by the guide sensor. C_ML corrects what is about to happen — the predicted residual error that the Kalman filter's linear model cannot capture. The Gain parameter blends these two correction streams into a single command that addresses both the present and the near future.
body.p_18: The system does not stop learning after initial training. It continues to record data throughout every session, which feeds a continuous feedback cycle.
body.p_19: Every ML prediction — the predicted error at T+60 seconds — is compared against the actual measured error 60 seconds later. This prediction-versus-reality comparison generates new labeled training data. Over time, this data is used to periodically retrain the model, allowing it to adapt to mount changes, seasonal temperature variations, and new mechanical behaviors that emerge as the equipment ages.
body.p_20: This feedback loop is what makes the hybrid system adaptive. A pure Kalman filter has a fixed physics model. In the hybrid system, the ML model is retrained periodically, so its predictions can follow changes in each mount over weeks and months of use.
body.p_21: Mathematically optimal for linear drift. Fast real-time response. Known convergence properties. Cannot learn mount-specific mechanical patterns. Limited to simple physical models.
body.p_22: Can learn complex patterns. Adapts to specific equipment. Requires large training datasets. No real-time guarantee. Risk of overfitting to training noise. Unstable without fallback.
body.p_23: Real-time Kalman correction plus ML prediction of recurring errors. Falls back to Kalman-only. Continuous learning loop. Adapts to mechanical changes over time. More complex than either approach alone.
body.p_24: Every 5 seconds: The Kalman filter processes the plate-solve measurement, smooths the noise, and estimates the immediate drift (position_kalman, velocity_kalman). At the same time, the ML model receives the sliding window of the last several minutes of feature data and produces a prediction of the form: "residual error of X pixels expected in 60 seconds, even with standard Kalman corrections."
body.p_25: Fusion: Instead of sending only the Kalman correction to the mount, the system combines both sources. The Kalman correction (C_K) handles the immediate, short-term error. The ML correction (C_ML) provides a proactive counter-command to negate the predicted future error.
body.p_26: The Gain parameter controls how aggressively the ML correction is applied. A gain of 0 disables ML entirely. A gain of 1.0 applies the full predicted correction. Tuning this parameter balances responsiveness against stability.
body.p_27: Training session: The ML model analyzes historical data and discovers the pattern: when Dec ≈ 45° and session time ≈ 300 seconds, an oscillation of +0.8 pixels will occur 60 seconds later. This pattern repeats consistently across multiple sessions at the same Declination.
body.p_28: Live session: You are imaging at Dec 45°. The Kalman filter is tracking a normal linear drift. At minute 4:50, the ML model — seeing the current position and elapsed time — predicts: "Warning: in 10 seconds (at t=300s), an oscillation will begin. I predict an error of +0.8 pixels at t=360s."
body.p_29: At minute 5:00: The Kalman filter begins to see a small deviation, which it initially attributes to noise. The ML prediction for this point has high confidence. The command sent to the mount is therefore not just the Kalman correction. It includes a small proactive counter-correction intended to cancel the predicted +0.8 pixel oscillation.
body.p_30: Result: In this scenario, the oscillation occurs but is largely offset by the proactive correction, and the guide star stays close to centre. The Kalman filter sees little drift and makes only a small update to its estimate. The star elongation that the defect would otherwise cause in a long exposure is reduced.
body.p_31: Complex mechanical compensation: The ML layer is designed to learn and reduce mechanical defects — gear oscillations, periodic error harmonics, backlash patterns, thermal flexure — that the Kalman filter's simple physics model cannot represent. These are the errors that cause star elongation in long exposures.
body.p_32: Long-exposure improvement: By predicting periodic errors and correcting them in advance, the hybrid system aims to keep tracking accuracy below one arcsecond in exposures that would otherwise show guiding artifacts. The expected benefit is largest in exposures longer than 5 minutes.
body.p_33: Adaptability: The model improves with time. As more sessions are recorded, the ML layer learns changes in the mount — seasonal thermal patterns, mechanical wear, new accessories that change the tube balance. Periodic retraining replaces manual retuning.
body.p_34: Complexity: The hybrid architecture is significantly more complex than a standalone Kalman filter. It requires training pipelines, feature engineering, model validation, and a fusion framework. The development and maintenance burden is substantially higher.
body.p_35: Training data requirements: The ML model needs hundreds of hours of high-quality, labeled guiding data to learn reliable patterns. Sessions with poor seeing, cloud cover, or equipment issues can introduce noise into the training set.
body.p_36: Overfitting risk: The model might memorize noise specific to the training sessions and fail to generalize to new conditions. The R² confidence gate mitigates this, but it remains a fundamental risk of any data-driven approach.
body.p_37: Stability concerns: ML corrections must be carefully bounded to prevent the proactive corrections from introducing new oscillations. The Gain parameter and correction clamping are essential safeguards against instability.

article.headline: Mount Modeling in HYBRID: Plate-Solve, Kalman, and Auto-Alignment
article.deck: Traditional mount modeling collects dozens of calibration points over hours. HYBRID uses a different approach: the Kalman filter state, updated by plate-solves and SYNC commands, serves as a continuously updated pointing model that needs no separate manual calibration run.

sidebar.stat_desc: Traditional pointing models need 30-100 star measurements. HYBRID starts estimating the pointing error from the first plate-solve, without a separate calibration run.

body.h2_1: The Traditional Approach: TPoint and Polynomial Models
body.h2_2: HYBRID's Approach: The Kalman Filter as Pointing Model
body.h2_3: The SYNC Command: How the Model Updates
body.h2_6: How HYBRID Handles Common Error Sources
body.h2_8: When to Use Traditional Mount Modeling
body.h3_1: The State Vector as Pointing Model
body.p_1: Every telescope mount has a pointing model — a mathematical description of where the mount thinks it is pointing versus where it actually points. Astronomers have long built these models by measuring the positions of calibration stars, one by one, across the sky. The result is a polynomial surface that maps desired coordinates to actual mount positions. The method is accurate, but it requires hours of manual work, and the work must be repeated whenever the mount moves, the temperature shifts, or the polar alignment drifts.
body.p_2: HYBRID Telescope Control does not use a traditional pointing model. Instead, it uses a plate-solve-based approach where the Kalman filter serves as a self-calibrating, real-time pointing model. Every 5 seconds, a plate-solve measures the actual pointing position. The Kalman filter estimates the error. A SYNC command tells the mount where it actually is. The pointing model is updated on every cycle without user input.
body.p_3: Traditional mount modeling works by collecting a set of calibration points across the sky. At each point, the user slews to a known star, measures the offset between where the mount thinks it is pointing and where the star actually is, and records the error. After collecting enough points — typically 30 to 100 — a polynomial surface is fitted to the error data. This surface becomes the pointing model: a lookup table that corrects for systematic errors like polar alignment offset, tube flexure, gear periodic error, and atmospheric refraction.
body.p_4: TPoint, developed by Software Bisque, is a widely used implementation of this approach. It uses polynomial fitting and can achieve arcsecond-class pointing accuracy across the entire sky. Professional observatories use TPoint variants for their mount calibration. The approach is well understood and well documented.
body.p_5: Polynomial models do have inherent limitations. They are static: the model does not change after calibration. If the temperature shifts and the tube flexes differently, the model loses accuracy. If the polar alignment drifts over a long session, the model loses accuracy. If the mount is moved to a different location, the model must be rebuilt from scratch. The model captures spatial patterns — how pointing errors vary across the sky — but not temporal patterns — how pointing errors change over time.
body.p_6: HYBRID replaces the static polynomial model with a dynamic Kalman state vector that is continuously updated by plate-solve measurements. The Kalman filter estimates four quantities for equatorial mounts: RA position error, RA velocity error, Dec position error, and Dec velocity error. These four states capture the essential pointing dynamics — where the mount is off and how fast the error is changing.
body.p_7: For Alt-Az mounts, the state vector extends to six elements: Az position error, Az velocity error, Alt position error, Alt velocity error, and two bias terms that capture the nonlinear coupling between the axes. The Extended Kalman filter handles the coordinate transformation through a numerical Jacobian, allowing the same Kalman framework to work for both mount geometries.
body.p_8: The Kalman state vector is not only a tracking correction; it also serves as the pointing model. The four (or six) state elements describe the mount's current pointing error in a compact, mathematical form. The state captures both the current offset and the rate of change, allowing the filter to predict where the mount will be in 5 seconds and apply a correction in advance.
body.p_9: This differs from a polynomial model. A polynomial tells you "at RA 6h, Dec +30°, the mount is off by +12 arcseconds in RA." The Kalman state tells you "right now, at whatever position you are, the mount is off by +12 arcseconds in RA, and the error is increasing at +0.3 arcseconds per second." The Kalman model is position-independent and time-adaptive.
body.p_10: The SYNC command is the bridge between measurement and model. When a plate-solve determines the actual pointing position, the SYNC command tells the mount: "You are here now." OnStep (the mount controller) then recalculates its internal pointing model, correcting systematic errors.
body.p_11: In HYBRID's architecture, the SYNC command is issued after every Kalman correction cycle. The flow is: plate-solve captures the actual position → Kalman computes the error and the correction → the correction is applied as a MoveAxis command → the SYNC command updates the mount's internal model. This creates a closed-loop system where the pointing model is continuously refined by real measurements.
body.p_12: A traditional calibration session involves slewing to specific stars, centering them in the eyepiece, recording the offset, and repeating 30-100 times. Each measurement is a static snapshot. The entire session takes 1-3 hours.
body.p_13: HYBRID's SYNC approach is continuous and automatic. Every plate-solve is effectively a calibration measurement — but instead of being recorded and processed later, it is applied immediately through the Kalman filter. In effect, calibration continues throughout the imaging session.
body.p_14: HYBRID's auto-alignment system combines plate-solving with the Kalman filter to measure polar alignment error automatically. The approach is based on the TVC (Takahashi Variation Correction) method, adapted for plate-solve-based measurement.
body.p_15: At session start, HYBRID takes a short exposure (3-5 seconds), plate-solves the image to determine the exact pointing coordinates, and compares them to the expected position. The offset between expected and actual position reveals the mount's initial pointing error — a combination of polar alignment error, tube alignment error, and any mechanical offset.
body.p_16: The system then slews to a second star, plate-solves again, and computes the pointing error at the new position. By comparing the error vectors at two different positions, the system can separate polar alignment error (which produces a characteristic pattern of RA/Dec offsets across the sky) from other error sources.
body.p_17: The process repeats iteratively: slew, plate-solve, measure offset, compute correction, SYNC. Each iteration refines the alignment. After 3-5 iterations, the system converges to within ±5 arcseconds of polar alignment — similar to a careful manual alignment with a dedicated polar scope, which typically takes around 30 minutes.
body.p_18: After the initial alignment, the Kalman filter takes over. Every subsequent plate-solve further refines the pointing model. Over the course of a long imaging session, the pointing accuracy is expected to improve as the Kalman filter accumulates more data about the mount's behavior at different positions, temperatures, and hour angles.
body.p_19: Polar alignment is the foundation of equatorial mount pointing. If the polar axis is not aligned with the celestial pole, every pointing model must compensate for the resulting field rotation — a systematic error that grows with hour angle and produces characteristic star trails in long exposures.
body.p_20: HYBRID implements a plate-solve-based polar alignment routine modeled on the TVC method. The algorithm measures the pointing offset at two positions in RA, computes the polar alignment error from the differential offset, and provides a correction vector that the user (or an automated focuser) can apply to the mount's azimuth and altitude adjusters.
body.p_21: The ±5 arcsecond accuracy relies on the same plate-solve measurements used by the tracking system. The plate solver uses star pattern matching with sub-arcsecond centroid accuracy, which provides the measurement precision needed for polar alignment.
body.p_22: Every mount has a characteristic set of error sources. Here is how HYBRID's dynamic approach handles each one, compared to traditional static modeling.
body.p_23: Polar alignment error produces a field rotation that depends on hour angle. A static model captures this at the time of calibration. HYBRID's Kalman filter tracks it continuously — as the hour angle changes, the filter's Dec velocity state adapts to the changing field rotation rate.
body.p_24: Periodic error is a sinusoidal wobble that repeats once per worm revolution. Traditional models capture the dominant harmonic. HYBRID's Kalman filter follows the periodic error as it occurs, including higher harmonics and amplitude variations that change with temperature and load, within the limits of its 5-second update interval.
body.p_25: Tube flexure changes with telescope orientation — pointing straight up produces different flexure than pointing at the horizon. A static model captures the average flexure. HYBRID's filter tracks flexure as a function of position, with the ML layer learning the mount-specific flexure pattern over time.
body.p_26: Refraction bends starlight upward, with the amount depending on altitude above the horizon. At 30° elevation, refraction is 1.7 arcminutes; at 10°, it exceeds 5 arcminutes. HYBRID computes refraction in real-time based on the target's altitude and local atmospheric conditions, incorporating it into the Kalman state model.
body.p_27: As temperature changes throughout the night, the telescope tube expands or contracts, shifting the focal plane and changing the optical alignment. A static model cannot adapt to this. HYBRID's Kalman filter tracks temperature-dependent drift as a slowly-varying bias state, adapting to thermal changes over the course of the session.
body.p_28: TVC-based plate-solve alignment achieves ±5 arcsecond polar alignment accuracy. Applied once at session start. Refined continuously by the Kalman filter.
body.p_29: Kalman state vector serves as the pointing model. Updated every 5 seconds by plate-solve measurements. Self-calibrating, drift-adaptive, no manual calibration run.
body.p_30: After each plate-solve, SYNC tells the mount where it actually is. OnStep recalculates its internal model. The mount's physical pointing model stays current.
body.p_31: The ML layer learns mount-specific patterns — periodic error harmonics, flexure curves, thermal drift profiles. Improves prediction accuracy over time.
body.p_32: HYBRID's dynamic approach is not always the best choice. Traditional mount modeling has specific advantages in certain scenarios:
body.p_33: On the test setup, HYBRID's dynamic approach reached a pointing accuracy of ±1-2 arcseconds RMS without a manual calibration run. Because the Kalman filter tracks temporal drift, pointing accuracy can improve over the course of a session as the filter accumulates more data about the mount's behavior.
body.p_34: The Kalman filter serves both as tracking correction and as pointing model. The state vector represents the current position-dependent error as well as temporal drift, rate of change and adaptive noise, which a static polynomial model does not represent. Using the Kalman state vector in place of the polynomial model was the main architectural decision.
body.p_35: A traditional pointing model is calibrated once and loses accuracy as conditions change. HYBRID's model is updated on every plate-solve, and every SYNC passes the update to the mount, so the model follows the current conditions.
body.p_36: The ASCOM SYNC command updates the mount's internal pointing model immediately, correcting systematic offsets without a full recalibration. HYBRID uses SYNC as the main mechanism for keeping the pointing model current.
body.p_37: Software correction cannot fully compensate for poor polar alignment. The TVC-based auto-alignment system reaches ±5 arcsecond accuracy, which is the starting point for the Kalman filter. Better polar alignment means better initial pointing, which means faster convergence and better tracking from the first frame.

article.headline: Closing the Roadmap: Six Phases From Acceleration States to Security Hardening
article.deck: Twenty items taken from this site's public roadmap pages, closed in one sequenced integration pass — new Kalman/EKF state terms, anisotropic ML noise tuning, per-mount transfer learning, an adaptive fusion gain, ASCOM-layer latency work, and a fix for credentials stored in plaintext. Along the way, a flaky test was found and fixed, and the CI configuration was found not to run most of the test suite.

sidebar.stat_desc: Six phases, no regressions recorded: every phase closed on a clean build-and-test pass before the next one started. 98 new tests were added, including 28 security tests; these were the first tests from HybridTelescopeControl.GUI.Tests to run in CI.

body.p_1: This site carries five pages of “Next Development Goals” — one each for the Kalman filter, the ML tracking layer, the security audit, the ASCOM/OnStep code path, and the ML–Kalman cognitive layer. Twenty roadmap items in total, scattered across five articles, accumulated over months of writing about what HYBRID does today rather than what it should do next. This entry is about closing all twenty of them in a single, deliberately sequenced integration pass — phase by phase, tested before moving on, documented as it went.
body.h2_1: Phase 0: Testing the Existing Math First
body.p_2: Before touching a single line of the production Kalman or Extended Kalman filter, the first phase built a cross-validation suite for math that had never been tested in isolation. Every matrix operation — multiply, inverse, transpose, the EKF's numerical Jacobian, the NIS innovation-gating computation — got a direct unit test. So did a near-zenith singularity check on the process-noise inflation, and a covariance-symmetry baseline recorded across 500 update cycles.
body.p_3: None of this changed behavior. The purpose was to have regression tests in place before later changes, so that any breakage they caused would be detected. Twenty-three tests were added in this phase, all of them regression guards for phases that had not been written yet.
body.h2_2: Phase 1: Acceleration States and Multi-Star Fusion
body.p_4: The 4-state linear Kalman filter (equatorial mounts) and the 6-state Extended Kalman filter (Alt-Az mounts) both gained acceleration terms — a second derivative that a constant-velocity model cannot represent. With it, the filters can model periodic-error harmonics and wind-induced disturbance rather than only react to them. In the EKF, the new acceleration terms drive the bias rate inside the nonlinear state transition, extending by one derivative the observability technique the filter already used to make bias estimable.
body.p_5: Multi-star tracking was added as a pre-filter fusion step rather than a joint multi-measurement rewrite of the update equations: several simultaneous guide-star observations are combined — MAD-based outlier rejection, then weighted averaging — into the single (RA error, Dec error) pair the filter already knows how to consume. This was a deliberate trade-off against a mathematically purer joint update, made to keep the filters' shared core math, used by every existing single-star call site, unchanged. It has no live caller yet: the plate-solve pipeline produces one solved position per cycle today, not per-star centroids, so this fusion primitive is waiting for a future multi-centroid measurement source.
body.p_6: The main difficulty in this phase was backward compatibility, not the math. GetStateVector() and GetCovarianceMatrix() keep returning their original 4-wide shape on both filters, because the web API and two UI diagnostic panels read them by raw array position, not only through the dimension-agnostic tuple accessors. Widening those two methods would have silently broken a documented API schema. Full-width data now lives behind new GetNativeStateVector()/GetNativeCovarianceMatrix() methods instead.
body.h2_3: Phase 2: Noise That Adapts Per Axis
body.p_7: Before this phase, the ML noise-tuning layer applied one combined scale to every state alike — a real disturbance on only one axis widened process noise on both axes and every derivative order together. Phase 2 replaced that with independent scaling per axis (RA/Dec, or Az/Alt) and per derivative order (position, velocity, acceleration). The acceleration-term scale is driven by the filter's own current acceleration estimate — which only exists because Phase 1 built it.
body.quote_1: The acceleration state built in Phase 1 was needed mainly as an input for Phase 2: a measured quantity against which to scale the acceleration noise.
body.p_8: Feature expansion: cloud cover is now fully wired from weather data the pipeline already fetches. Focuser temperature and mount current draw were added as opt-in callbacks with safe defaults, since no standard ASCOM Alpaca telescope property exposes current draw; this is a limitation of the protocol, not an omission.
body.p_9: Model versioning with automatic rollback: every retrain now backs up the outgoing model before overwriting it, and if the freshly trained model's R² regresses meaningfully below the one it's replacing, the previous version is restored automatically instead of leaving tracking on a worse model.
body.p_10: Cross-mount transfer learning: model storage is now keyed by a sanitized mount identity instead of one shared path, and a mount with no trained model yet seeds itself from the most recently trained sibling mount rather than starting from an empty buffer.
body.p_11: “Online learning” was implemented as an approximation: ML.NET's SDCA trainer has no incremental-fit API, so periodic full retrains continue. What Phase 3 added is a rolling self-prediction memory — each training sample now carries what the model predicted just before that observation — which gives the retrained model temporal continuity across sessions. It is documented as an approximation, not as true online learning.
body.p_12: Multi-target feature sharing indexes training history by declination band and seeds a new target from the nearest band with data — live-wired directly into the start-tracking call, since the target's declination was already sitting right there in the method signature.
body.p_13: Adaptive gain scheduling replaced a fixed 70/30 Kalman/ML blend — used at all four fusion call sites in the tracking controller — with a weight computed from ML confidence, current wind speed, and recent tracking-error stability. Worse seeing conditions shift the blend toward the ML layer, which takes weather data as input, unlike the Kalman model; a volatile recent error history shifts it back toward the more conservative filter output.
body.p_14: An explainability layer surfaces ML.NET's permutation feature importance so that a future panel could show which features drive a given drift prediction. One caveat: it compiles against the installed ML.NET package (an initial assumption about the API shape was wrong and the compiler caught it), but it has not yet been run against a live trained model; that needs a real training session to verify end to end.
body.p_15: ASCOM Alpaca is a REST protocol, not WebSocket, so the roadmap's “WebSocket bridge” item was reinterpreted as HTTP keep-alive tuning. This revealed a specific issue: .NET Framework defaults to 2 connections per host, which would have serialized the new concurrent RA/Dec dispatch as soon as anything else shared that host. The limit was raised to 10. The RA-axis and Dec-axis motor corrections are now sent concurrently rather than sequentially; this is also what “multi-command batching” came to mean, since Alpaca's REST design cannot combine two endpoints into one transaction.
body.p_16: A rate-smoothing filter and a predictive sync-timing scheduler were both added as small, pure, standalone functions rather than logic inside the tracking loop, so that the math can be unit-tested without a real mount or a real socket.
body.h2_7: Phase 6: Credential Encryption and Audit Logging
body.p_17: The security phase included a finding from the initial research pass, made before work on the six phases began: webserver_config.json stored the web server's username, password, and MCP API key in plaintext, including the unchanged factory-default password. DPAPI-based encryption now protects that file at rest, and an existing plaintext file is migrated to the encrypted format the next time it is saved.
body.p_18: Audit logging reused the project's existing structured logger rather than standing up a second parallel logging system — login success and failure, account lockouts, logout, remote command execution, and configuration changes now write to a persistent, taggable trail instead of only ever flashing past as a UI message.
body.p_19: A further finding concerned the CI workflow rather than the security code: the GitHub Actions pipeline only ran one test project. The tests from every phase of this integration — all 259 of them, the entire Kalman/EKF math suite, the ML pipeline tests, the ASCOM and security tests — were in a project that CI did not run. Adding one workflow step fixed this.
body.p_20: Not everything was wired all the way through, and the gaps are documented. Focuser-temperature, mount-current-draw, and mount-identity callbacks exist as working infrastructure with safe defaults, but connecting them to a live source requires a larger constructor and threading change to the tracking controller that did not belong in this pass. The explainability layer's permutation-importance output has not been checked against a real trained model. A post-flip mount re-sync still runs outside the new predictive sync scheduler, because the class that triggers it does not hold a reference to the tracking controller today.
body.p_21: The same approach applied in every phase: implement the feature, connect it to live code where that is low-risk, and document what is deferred and why, rather than forcing a larger change into the pass or dropping the item.
body.p_22: Six phases, ninety-eight new tests, no regressions carried from one phase into the next:
body.h3_1: A Flaky Test Is Still a Bug
body.p_23: One isolation test in the EKF suite asserted exact equality between two separately constructed filter instances. The EKF reads the system clock internally for sidereal time, so two instances built microseconds apart can diverge by a small but non-zero, timing-driven amount. The test failed once and passed on immediate rerun, which is typical of a flaky test. The fix was a tolerance loosened by nine orders of magnitude, with a comment explaining why, so that the tolerance is understood as intentional.
body.h3_2: The Pipeline Is Part of the Test Suite
body.p_24: A test suite that CI does not run provides no protection, even when the CI check shows green for another project. Finding and closing that gap was one of the more significant results of this pass.
body.p_25: Seven phases (zero through six), each one gated on a clean build-and-test pass before the next started, each documented in its own specification addendum. Changing everything at once would have been faster, but it would have made it much harder to attribute a failure to a specific change.
