article.headline: Kalman Filter Fixes: Gain Dimensions, EKF Output and Matrix Inversion
article.deck: A review of the tracking subsystem found three problems in the Kalman filter code. The fixes correct the gain-matrix multiplication for equatorial mounts, connect the EKF correction to the mount output for Alt-Az mounts, and generalize the matrix inversion routine to any matrix size.

sidebar.stat_desc: Two filter code paths fixed and one matrix routine generalized. The changes affect tracking on both equatorial and Alt-Az mounts.

sections.architecture_title: The Architecture: Three Layers of Tracking

body.p_1: On June 10, 2026, a review of the HYBRID Telescope Control tracking subsystem found three issues in the mathematical implementation. Two of them affected equatorial and Alt-Az drift correction; the third limited the matrix inversion routine to small matrices. Because the tracking loop catches exceptions and continues, the mount kept tracking throughout, but without the Kalman filter's predictive corrections.
body.p_2: HYBRID's tracking system operates on three layers that run simultaneously. Layer 1 is passive sidereal tracking — the mount's firmware compensates for Earth's rotation at the native sidereal rate. Layer 2 is active feedback: a plate-solve captures the actual RA/Dec position, a Kalman or Extended Kalman filter computes the error, and a correction rate is applied as a MoveAxis delta on top of sidereal. Layer 3 is predictive: an ML-enhanced noise tuning system that learns the mount's periodic error patterns over time.
body.p_3: The Kalman filter was chosen for equatorial mounts because their tracking geometry is linear in RA/Dec — a 4-state model (RA position, RA velocity, Dec position, Dec velocity) captures the essential dynamics. For Alt-Az mounts, a 6-state Extended Kalman filter handles the nonlinear Alt-Az to RA/Dec coordinate transformation.
body.p_4: Before this fix, Alt-Az mounts received no EKF correction. The EKF's model itself was correct: the bias states were estimated correctly, the Jacobian mapping was valid, and the correction was computed with consistent dimensions. The fix connects the computation to the output path so that the EKF correction reaches the mount hardware.
body.p_5: The replacement implements a general n×n Gauss-Jordan elimination with partial pivoting, a standard numerical linear algebra routine that works for any matrix size. The state vector can therefore grow without changes to the core linear algebra code.
body.p_6: Release build: 0 errors. Both filters now apply corrections to mount tracking on every plate-solve cycle. The equatorial Kalman filter applies its gain with the correct dimensions. The Alt-Az EKF transmits its computed correction to the mount. The Gauss-Jordan inverse handles any matrix dimension.
body.p_7: Besides correcting the mathematics, the changes add checks that make similar problems easier to detect.
body.p_8: Runtime dimension validation now accompanies all matrix operations in the Kalman filter. If a future state vector expansion (acceleration states, environmental parameters, or multi-star tracking) introduces a dimension error, it is reported at the point of computation rather than surfacing later as a failure.
body.p_9: The Alt-Az Extended Kalman filter correction path is now connected end to end: plate-solve measurement, state estimation, Jacobian mapping and mount command. This matches the intended design for nonlinear mount tracking.
body.p_10: The tracking loop's exception handling, which keeps the mount tracking during transient numerical issues, was kept. The fixes change the primary code path and leave the fallback in place for unexpected conditions.
body.p_11: Each fix was checked with the unit tests listed above and the full GUI test suite.
body.p_12: With the Kalman gain matrix applied correctly, equatorial mounts now receive the filter's predictive corrections. The tracking loop no longer falls back to sidereal-only mode because of the dimension mismatch, which should give more consistent drift correction on equatorial mounts.
body.p_13: The EKF correction path is now complete from computation to mount command. Alt-Az mounts now use the nonlinear tracking model, including field rotation compensation and atmospheric refraction estimation. The aim is to bring Alt-Az tracking closer to equatorial performance.
body.p_14: The generalized matrix inversion routine handles any dimension, providing a safety margin for future state vector growth. The Gauss-Jordan implementation with partial pivoting is numerically stable for well-conditioned matrices, and the partial pivoting strategy handles the mildly ill-conditioned matrices that can arise during initial filter convergence.
body.p_15: The tracking loop's exception handling (catch the error, continue with sidereal tracking) kept the mount tracking while the defects were present, so imaging sessions were not interrupted. It also hid the defects. Silent fallback is suitable for transient issues, but it should be paired with logging that makes persistent issues visible for review.
body.p_16: The 131-test suite validated the surrounding infrastructure — ASCOM wrappers, UI state management, session persistence. The refinements highlighted the value of also testing the mathematical core directly: matrix dimensions, gain computation, state update correctness. This led to the addition of dedicated mathematical validation tests.
body.p_17: The matrix dimension refinement demonstrated that explicit dimensional analysis — tracking the dimensions of every matrix operation through the computation — serves as both verification and documentation. Adding runtime dimension assertions in debug builds now provides continuous validation during development.
body.p_18: The matrix inversion change is not required by current functionality. It removes a limit that would otherwise have to be addressed when the state vector grows to support new tracking features.
body.p_19: The main fix concerns the Kalman filter's Update method, which applies the measurement correction in the equatorial tracking system. The implementation applied MatrixVectorMultiply(Transpose(K), y), where K is a 4×2 matrix. Transposing a 4×2 produces a 2×4 matrix. Multiplying that by the 2-element innovation vector y yields a 2-vector. But the state vector is 4 elements. The dimension mismatch triggered an exception on every cycle; the tracking loop caught it and continued with sidereal-only tracking.
body.p_20: The Kalman gain matrix K is computed as P·HT·S-1, where P is the 4×4 covariance, H is the 2×4 measurement Jacobian, and S is the 2×2 innovation covariance. K is therefore 4×2. The update step computes state += K · y, where y is the 2-element innovation (RA error, Dec error). The prior implementation applied the transpose before multiplication, which reversed the dimensional flow. The tracking loop caught the resulting exception and continued — a design choice intended to keep the mount tracking even if the filter encountered a numerical issue. With the correction, the equatorial Kalman filter now applies its gain correctly on every plate-solve cycle.
body.p_21: The Extended Kalman filter for Alt-Az mounts computed its optimal tracking rate in GetOptimalTrackingRate. The method calculated azimuth and altitude rates from the EKF's estimated drift bias states, mapped them to RA/Dec via a numerical Jacobian, and returned the correction. That computed correction was not the value sent to the mount. The fix makes it the transmitted value, which completes the EKF correction path for Alt-Az tracking.
body.p_22: KalmanFilter.MatrixInverse previously handled inputs up to 2×2 dimensions. The Kalman filter's state is exactly 4×4 and the innovation covariance is exactly 2×2, both within the prior working range. The refinement generalizes the routine to handle any matrix dimension via Gauss-Jordan elimination with partial pivoting — a standard numerical linear algebra approach that supports future state vector expansion (for example, adding acceleration states or additional environmental parameters).

article.headline: How the Voice Control Pipeline Connects to 47 Telescope Tools
article.deck: The architecture of the conversational voice pipeline (Whisper, Silero VAD and the Model Context Protocol) and how a spoken command becomes telescope motion, which the project reports takes under three seconds.

sidebar.stat_desc: Exposed via the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that Anthropic's Claude uses to connect to tools. Any MCP-compatible AI client can call them.

body.p_1: HYBRID Telescope Control uses conversational voice control as its primary interaction model. A command such as "slew to M31, plate solve, and start imaging for 90 minutes" is carried out as a sequence of mount and camera operations. The voice pipeline has five stages (capture, transcribe, parse, dispatch, respond), and the project reports a time from microphone audio to telescope motion of under three seconds.
body.p_2: The system supports three interchangeable voice backends: Claude Desktop via MCP for cloud AI reasoning, a local llama.cpp server for fully offline operation at remote observatories, and a built-in Whisper grammar parser as a zero-dependency fallback. The user picks the mode that fits their session. The hardware commands are identical regardless of which backend processes the voice input.
body.p_3: The voice pipeline begins at the microphone. Audio is captured using Python's sounddevice library with numpy for buffer management. Silero VAD (Voice Activity Detection) monitors the audio stream and detects when the user is speaking — this replaces wake-word detection, which proved unreliable near cooling fans and wind noise. Push-to-talk is more reliable in an observatory environment.
body.p_4: The STT engine uses faster-whisper, a CTranslate2 port of OpenAI's Whisper model, running the small.en variant. It was chosen for its balance of accuracy and speed — the small model transcribes in near-real-time on modern hardware while handling the disfluencies and hesitations of natural speech.
body.p_5: 62 built-in STT corrections handle Whisper's most common astronomical transcription errors. "M31" and "am 31" both map to the canonical "M31". "Pleiadies" maps to "M45". "Orion nebula" maps to "M42". These corrections run before the grammar parser, so the parser only sees clean canonical names.
body.p_6: goto_target, goto_coordinates, park, unpark, find_home, stop_move, move_axis, emergency_stop, abort_slew
body.p_7: quick_capture, start_imaging, stop_imaging, pause_imaging, resume_imaging, autofocus, plate_solve
body.p_8: start_tracking, stop_tracking, get_tracking_status, get_kalman_state, get_ml_status, start_advanced_tracking
body.p_9: add_target, get_night_plan, start_scheduler, stop_scheduler, skip_target, get_scheduler_targets
body.p_10: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard (Anthropic, 2024) that gives AI assistants access to external tools via a structured interface. HYBRID exposes 47 telescope tools through an MCP server built on .NET 8. Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot, or any MCP-compatible client can discover and call these tools.
body.p_11: The voice pipeline runs in Python because its key libraries (faster-whisper, Silero VAD, gTTS) are Python libraries without direct C# equivalents of similar performance. The main application runs in C# because WPF is the native Windows UI framework and ASCOM integration is C#-native. The two sides communicate through subprocess IPC: Python processes audio and produces a command string; C# receives it via stdout and dispatches it to ASCOM. There is no shared state, no DLL conflict and no runtime version issue.
body.p_12: The telescope parser is a grammar-based system defined in telescope_grammar.py with parser tables generated at build time. It maps natural language phrases to canonical actions — 55 distinct actions covering mount control, camera operations, focuser, tracking, scheduling, weather, session management, and emergency procedures.
body.p_13: Each action supports 3 to 8 natural language phrase variants. "Slew to M31", "go to M31", "point at Andromeda", "track M31" all map to the same goto_target action. Fuzzy matching handles minor misrecognitions. The parser returns a canonical action name, target type, and parsed parameters — the dispatcher does not need to understand natural language.
body.p_14: MCP also supports tool chaining. A user can say "slew to M81, plate solve, autofocus, and start imaging for 30 minutes with 180-second exposures", and the AI breaks this into a sequence of MCP tool calls: goto_target, plate_solve, autofocus, start_imaging. Each tool call is dispatched to the ASCOM API. The AI handles the orchestration; the hardware handles the motion.
body.p_15: Three principles guided the voice architecture. First, reliability over intelligence — push-to-talk over wake-word, grammar parsing over free-form NLU, deterministic dispatch over probabilistic reasoning. Second, graceful degradation — if Claude is unavailable, the local LLM takes over; if the LLM is unavailable, the grammar parser handles it; if the grammar fails, the user falls back to clicks. Third, transparent failure — every voice command produces visible feedback in the UI and spoken TTS response, so the user always knows what happened and why.

article.headline: Activating the ML Tracking Layer: Dual-Axis SDCA Regression
article.deck: The SDCA training pipeline trained a single-axis regressor, which left most prediction fields empty and kept the ML layer inactive. Extending it to dual-axis prediction, with an R² confidence score and noise scaling, lets the ML layer take part in tracking.

sidebar.stat_desc: The ML confidence field now carries the R² value of the trained model. The Confidence > 0.5 gate engages when the model explains more than half of the variance in the drift data.

body.p_1: Since v1.2.0, HYBRID Telescope Control has included an ML tracking layer: a machine learning component intended to adapt the Kalman filter's noise parameters to observed drift patterns. The 24-feature extraction, the SDCA regression engine, the confidence gate and the noise scaling formulas were in place. A review in June 2026 found that the training pipeline trained only the RA axis, so the ML layer had no effect on tracking. This release extends the pipeline to dual-axis regression.
body.p_2: HYBRID operates three tracking layers simultaneously. Understanding the full architecture clarifies the ML layer's role within the system:
body.p_3: Layer 3 observes the Kalman filter's prediction errors over time, trains a regression model on the 24-feature vector extracted from each plate-solve cycle, and dynamically adjusts the filter's process and measurement noise covariance. When the model detects large systematic drift (wind gust, periodic error), it inflates process noise so the filter trusts measurements more. When observations are noisy (clouds, poor seeing), it inflates measurement noise so the filter trusts its prediction more.
body.p_4: The confidence gate now receives the model's R² value. When R² exceeds 0.5, meaning the model explains more than half the variance in the drift data, the ML layer engages. When R² is below 0.5, the filter operates with baseline Kalman/EKF parameters. The ML layer therefore only contributes when its predictions meet this statistical threshold.
body.p_5: Both scales are hard-clamped to [0.1, 10.0]. This prevents covariance collapse (scale approaching zero, filter ignores everything) and covariance explosion (scale approaching infinity, filter ignores nothing). The clamp keeps the noise scaling within bounds regardless of what the ML model predicts.
body.p_6: The ML model processes a 24-feature vector at each training step, extracted from the plate-solve history:
body.p_7: These features describe each measurement: where the mount is pointing, what time it is, what the weather is doing, and how the filter has been performing. The SDCA regressor learns which features correlate with drift, and uses that correlation to predict future drift from the current feature vector.
body.p_8: The ML tracking layer is now active. In the first session, it collects training data, trains both RA and Dec models, evaluates R², and engages if the threshold is met. In later sessions, saved models load at start-up, and the confidence gate can open from the first plate solve if the saved R² meets the threshold. The noise parameters are then adjusted from the mount's observed behavior on each plate-solve cycle.
body.p_9: The dual-axis extension changes the structure of the ML pipeline in three ways.
body.p_10: The training pipeline now populates all five prediction fields that the consumer code expects. The implementation now matches what the consuming code was written for.
body.p_11: Training separate models for RA and Dec drift reflects the fact that these error sources have different characteristics. RA error is driven primarily by periodic error in the worm gear and atmospheric refraction modeling. Dec error is driven by polar alignment error, flexure, and wind loading. Independent models are intended to capture these different dynamics better than a single combined model.
body.p_12: With the ML layer active, noise tuning responds to current conditions as described below.
body.p_13: With the confidence gate operational, the Kalman filter's noise covariance matrices now adapt to current conditions. On steady nights with good seeing, the model's R² is expected to exceed the threshold, and the filter uses the ML-adjusted noise parameters. On turbulent nights, if R² falls below the threshold, the filter uses baseline parameters, so a poorly fitting model does not influence tracking.
body.p_14: Saved models load at session start, providing ML augmentation from the first plate solve. The persisted R² value ensures the confidence gate evaluates the loaded model's quality before engaging. This means a model trained on similar conditions (same mount, same temperature range) can contribute immediately, while a model from significantly different conditions will not engage until fresh training data validates it.
body.p_15: Legacy single-axis models import safely, with the RA model reused for Dec prediction as a fallback. Existing installations keep their trained models when they upgrade.
body.p_16: The design of the ML layer (the 24-feature vector, the confidence gate, the noise scaling formulas) did not need to change. The defect was in the training pipeline, which trained only one axis. Once it was identified, the fix was limited to the training code.
body.p_17: Struct fields defaulting to zero produced no errors, no exceptions, no test failures. The system ran correctly — it just didn't run the ML pathway. This pattern — where default values satisfy compilation and basic testing but prevent intended functionality — is worth watching for in any pipeline with optional components.
body.p_18: The R² confidence gate behaved as intended. Rather than always engaging the ML layer (which could degrade tracking if the model is poorly trained), the gate requires the model to reach a minimum statistical quality before it influences the filter. The same approach is useful in other adaptive systems.
body.p_19: The SDCA (Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent) pipeline in ML.NET originally trained a single-output regressor with the label RADrift. ML.NET's prediction engine populated the Score field with the RA drift prediction. However, the consumer code expected five fields: RADrift, DecDrift, Confidence, ProcessNoise, and MeasurementNoise. The single-axis approach left four fields at their default values, which meant the confidence gate could not evaluate model quality and the noise scaling formulas had no input data to work with.
body.p_20: The original implementation trained a single SDCA regressor on the RA drift label. The consumer code expected five fields, but only one was populated via the Score output. The other four were struct fields with zero defaults. The Confidence field, designed to represent the model's R² (coefficient of determination), remained at zero — which meant the > 0.5 gate was permanently closed and the ML noise-tuning pathway was not engaged.
body.p_21: The extension trains two SDCA regressors per filter — one with Label=RADrift, one with Label=DecDrift — sharing the same feature concatenation. Two PredictionEngine instances are created, one per axis. A new BuildPrediction helper assembles a fully populated prediction:
body.p_22: The noise scaling formulas translate ML predictions into Kalman filter tuning adjustments. Process noise scale is computed as clamp(1 + |drift|/baseline, 0.1, 10.0). When the ML model detects large drift, the scale increases, telling the filter to trust measurements more. Measurement noise scale is clamp(1 + scatter/baseline, 0.1, 10.0). When observations are noisy, the scale increases, telling the filter to trust its prediction more.
body.p_23: Position: RA/Dec errors, rates, hour angle, altitude, azimuth
body.p_24: Temporal: Timestamp, UT hour, LST hour, Julian date fraction
body.p_26: Statistical: Error std dev, drift trend, innovation magnitude
body.p_27: The extension also addressed two operational concerns. First, thread safety: the WebServer thread calls PredictDriftML while the UI thread can trigger ForceRetrain, and the EKF retrains on a background Task. A modelLock guards engine swaps and paired Predict calls to prevent torn reads. Second, persistence: both models are saved side by side (kalman_ml_model.zip + _dec.zip for KF; ekf_ml_model.zip + _dec.zip for EKF). A freshly loaded model reads the persisted R² from metrics.json so the confidence gate works from the first plate solve without retraining.
body.p_28: The modelLock mutex ensures that model swaps — whether triggered by retraining, session load, or API request — do not produce torn reads across threads. This is particularly important for the WebServer thread, which calls PredictDriftML on every plate-solve cycle while the UI or background tasks may trigger retraining simultaneously.

article.headline: Security Audit: Six Fixes Across Four Subsystems
article.deck: An audit of the voice, camera, mount and web subsystems led to changes in authentication defaults, meridian flip verification, process shutdown, session file writes and FITS handling, delivered in nine commits.

sidebar.stat_desc: A structured audit across four subsystems: voice, camera/imaging, mount/ASCOM/scheduler, and web/MCP/cloud. Each finding was checked against the source code, and each fix was build-tested.

body.p_1: On June 10, 2026, a security audit of four HYBRID Telescope Control subsystems (voice, camera/imaging, mount/ASCOM/scheduler, and web/MCP/cloud) led to changes in six areas of the codebase. Each area was reviewed against the source code, and each finding was confirmed as an actual implementation gap, not a theoretical risk, before it was classified. The fixes were made in nine commits, each verified by a successful build.
body.p_2: Security reviews are a routine part of development, particularly for software that controls physical hardware. This one covered default settings, authentication paths and edge cases.
body.p_3: The scheduler's meridian flip is a safety-relevant operation that rotates the mount 180° as the target crosses the meridian, keeping the telescope on the same side of the pier. The change adds verification: the system now waits for slew completion, verifies that the pier side changed, and halts the session if verification fails.
body.p_4: Scheduler calls re-slew to same target. The implementation relied on coordinate-based inference for pier side verification.
body.p_5: The audit resulted in the following structural changes.
body.p_6: Web authentication is now secure by default: the system requires explicit configuration to disable authentication, rather than explicit configuration to enable it. The same default applies to web server features added later.
body.p_7: The meridian flip now includes verification of slew completion and pier side, and halts the session on failure. Previously the flip was assumed to succeed; now it is checked, which matters for unattended observatory operation.
body.p_8: The lock + atomic temp-then-move pattern for session state is a standard data integrity technique that prevents corruption during concurrent writes or unexpected shutdowns. This pattern can be applied to other configuration files as the system grows.
body.p_9: Each change affects a specific operating scenario.
body.p_10: With the authentication and CORS changes, remote observatory operation via ngrok tunnels is authenticated by default. Authentication is enabled automatically when remote access starts, without manual security configuration.
body.p_11: The meridian flip changes add verification steps that address a serious failure mode in automated imaging: the telescope approaching the pier. By requiring pier side verification and halting on failure, the system prioritizes physical safety over imaging continuity.
body.p_12: Clean process termination prevents orphaned processes from holding GPU memory and system resources. This matters most for long unattended imaging sessions, where resource leaks could degrade performance over time.
body.p_13: The embedded web server's AuthEnabled flag defaulted to false. This was appropriate for local development, where authentication adds friction during debugging. With the change, SetAuthEnabled is activated automatically when an ngrok tunnel is started for remote access, so remote access is not left unauthenticated.
body.p_14: The CORS configuration was also changed. The IsLocalRequest check now treats X-Forwarded-* headers as WAN traffic, so tunneled requests are correctly identified as non-local. The /mcp/* endpoint requires non-local origin plus Bearer token or API key, which adds a second layer of protection for the AI tool interface.
body.p_15: SetAuthEnabled is now forced ON at both tunnel-start paths (and OFF on stop). The auth gate is scoped to non-local /api/ and /ws/ endpoints. IsLocalRequest now treats X-Forwarded-* headers as WAN traffic. The /mcp/* endpoint requires non-local origin plus Bearer token or API key.
body.p_16: Scheduler calls ExecuteMeridianFlipAsync. Waits for slew completion. Verifies pier side changed via ASCOM driver. Halts session on verification failure.
body.p_17: SafeParkAsync was also changed: it now calls Abort + StopTracking before Park, with a StopAllAxes fallback if Park fails. When the ASCOM driver returns "Unknown" for pier side, the flip no longer relies on inference; it halts the session instead, so the mount is not moved on an unverified pier side.
body.p_18: Two changes addressed process management and data integrity. Voice bridge Python processes and the local llama.cpp server now terminate cleanly on app close, with StopLocalLlmServer via taskkill /F /T /PID integrated into the shutdown sequence. These processes therefore no longer keep running after the application exits.
body.p_19: Session state persistence now uses atomic writes. session_state.json, which holds open tabs, todo progress, and conversation history, is written with a lock + atomic temp-then-move pattern: write to a .tmp file, rename on success. A partial write therefore cannot replace the real file, which protects session data if power is lost or the application restarts during a write.
body.p_20: The FITS reader used by the autofocus pipeline was extended to handle multi-block headers, BZERO/BSCALE scaling, and all BITPIX values. The implementation delegates FITS reading to ImageLoader, which supports these FITS variants. Autofocus measurements are therefore based on correctly scaled pixel data for FITS files from different camera drivers.
body.p_21: The tunnel-start operation was changed to prevent UI blocking. The prior implementation used tunnelStartTask.GetAwaiter().GetResult(), which blocked the dispatcher thread. The new implementation uses fire-and-forget Task.Run with async AddMessage on completion, returning "starting..." immediately and reporting the result asynchronously. The zenith azimuth rate was also capped at 5 deg/s to prevent commanding rates that exceed the mount's physical capability at the zenith singularity.

feature.headline: Project Overview: From First Commit to v1.2.2 PRO
feature.deck: An overview of HYBRID Telescope Control, a Windows telescope control application with conversational voice control, from late 2024 to June 2026: 200+ source files, 347+ tests, and a release that combines voice control, AI tool integration and predictive tracking.

body.p_1: HYBRID Telescope Control is a Windows application for operating an amateur telescope by voice. A command such as "slew to M31, plate solve, and start imaging for 90 minutes" is carried out as a sequence of mount and camera operations. It is not intended to replace established imaging suites such as NINA or SGP. Its interaction model is different: voice-first control, combined with AI tool orchestration through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
body.p_2: Development started in late 2024. By June 2026 the codebase comprised 200+ C# source files, 347+ unit tests, 47 MCP tools and 55+ voice actions, and a security audit had been completed in nine commits. This article summarizes how the project reached that state.
body.p_3: The starting point was practical: operating telescope software at -5°C while wearing gloves is awkward. Each click means removing a glove, finding the right menu and hitting a small target, then putting the glove back on. Voice control addresses this directly and improves usability in the observing workflow, beyond simple convenience.
body.p_4: Simple voice commands are not sufficient on their own. A wake-word system that responds to "Hey Telescope" can handle "go to M31" but not "slew to M31, plate solve, center it, autofocus, and start imaging for two hours with 180-second exposures." Multi-step commands require an AI model that can plan the sequence. The Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic in 2024, provides a standard way for an AI assistant to discover and call telescope tools.
body.p_5: First commit. Basic ASCOM mount control, WPF UI, no voice. Voice commands were planned from the start.
body.p_6: Python voice bridge with faster-whisper STT, Silero VAD, gTTS feedback. Three backend modes: Claude Desktop MCP, local llama.cpp, Whisper grammar. 55+ actions, 210+ phrase variants.
body.p_7: 47 telescope tools exposed via Model Context Protocol. Claude Desktop can drive the telescope directly. Tool chaining: "goto + plate solve + autofocus + image" in one sentence.
body.p_8: Passive sidereal + active Kalman/EKF feedback + predictive ML noise tuning. Equatorial (4-state KF) and Alt-Az (6-state EKF) filters. Reported tracking error: under 2 arcseconds RMS.
body.p_9: GPU-accelerated stacking (ILGPU), star alignment (triangle matching + RANSAC), background extraction (RBF + polynomial), drizzle, narrowband, SPCC color calibration.
body.p_10: First public release, with the feature set described above. Announced with a press kit and forum posts.
body.p_11: Security audit in 9 commits. ML tracking layer activated. Kalman filter fixes. 131 tests passing.
body.p_12: The application is built on three technology layers. The main application is C# targeting .NET Framework 4.8 with WPF for the UI: 200+ source files organized into a 7-project Visual Studio solution. The voice pipeline runs in Python 3.11 (bundled in the installer) because faster-whisper, Silero VAD, and gTTS are Python libraries without direct C# equivalents of similar performance. The MCP server runs on .NET 8, separate from the main application, and exposes 47 tools via the Model Context Protocol.
body.p_13: Several defects found in 2026 did not cause visible failures, because graceful degradation hid them. The Kalman filter's matrix dimension issue was caught by the tracking loop's exception handling, which kept the mount tracking but without the filter's corrections. The EKF computed its optimal rate, but the output path was not connected to the mount command layer. The ML layer's training pipeline trained only the RA axis and needed extension to dual-axis regression before the ML layer could engage.
body.p_14: All three issues shared a common pattern: the system continued to function, tests passed, and no exceptions surfaced to the user. The graceful degradation design, intended to keep the mount tracking during transient numerical issues, made the defects invisible in normal operation. They were found through systematic code review and mathematical validation.
body.p_15: The meridian flip change added verification steps for physical safety. The scheduler now verifies that the pier side changed and halts the session if verification fails. This matters for unattended operation, where no one is present to stop the mount.
body.p_16: In use so far, voice control has been most useful in three scenarios. First, the most common sequence: goto + plate solve + start imaging, given as one command, after which the observer can leave the scope to run. Second, cold-weather operation: changing exposure, filter, or target mid-sequence without touching the laptop. Third, accessibility: observers with mobility limitations, or those doing public outreach with groups around a scope, get a more natural way to interact.
body.p_17: Voice is less suited for precise numerical input, complex filter trees, and noisy environments. It does not replace click-based interaction; it complements it in the cases where hands-free operation is more practical.
body.p_18: v1.2.0 was released with working functionality. The later audit found defects that only a deliberate review would uncover.
body.p_19: Hardware commands must verify their effect. "The flip probably worked" is not acceptable when the alternative is equipment damage.
body.p_20: The development trace log was used extensively during the audit. A structured review process was useful at this codebase size (200+ files).
body.p_22: 2 hardening areas — web auth, meridian flip
body.p_23: 3 improvements — process lifecycle, session persistence, FITS handling
body.p_25: The web authentication change was the main security fix. The AuthEnabled = false default was appropriate for local development, where typing a password for every API call during debugging adds unnecessary friction. With the change, authentication is activated automatically when the ngrok tunnel is started for remote access, so remote access is not left unauthenticated.
body.p_26: AuthEnabled = false was a development convenience. The change made secure-by-default the rule for authentication settings.
body.p_27: The roadmap includes comment-mode surgical edits (click on any part of a generated artifact and ask for changes), a skill marketplace (od skills install), one-command initialization (npx od init), and a packaged Electron build with bundled sidecars. The project is MIT-licensed and open to contribution.

article.headline: The Languages Behind the Observatory
article.deck: Five programming languages, two runtime environments, one telescope control system. A map of where the code lives and why each language was chosen.

sidebar.stat_desc: C#, Python, C++, HTML/CSS/JS, PowerShell/Batch/NSIS — each used for a specific part of the system.

sections.python_title: Python — The Voice and the Post-Processor
sections.build_title: PowerShell / Batch / NSIS — Build and Deploy

body.h2_2: Python — The Voice and the Post-Processor
body.h2_5: PowerShell / Batch / NSIS — Build and Deploy
body.p_1: HYBRID Telescope Control uses five programming languages, each assigned to a specific subsystem. C# runs the application and hardware integration. Python handles voice recognition and image processing scripts. C++ provides native math routines. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript build the remote-access web dashboard. PowerShell, Batch, and NSIS handle build, packaging, and deployment.
body.p_2: Each language boundary follows from a technical requirement: WPF requires C#, faster-whisper requires Python, ASCOM integration is built on .NET, the web dashboard runs in the browser, and the installer uses Windows-native tooling. For the end user the split is not visible — they install and run one application.
body.p_3: C# is the primary language, comprising roughly 80% of the codebase. The main application — every UI tab, every ASCOM wrapper, every tracking algorithm, every image processing pipeline, the web server, the scheduler, the session manager — is written in C# targeting .NET Framework 4.8 with WPF for the user interface.
body.p_4: The choice of C# was driven by three constraints. First, the ASCOM ecosystem is built on .NET, and its client libraries for Alpaca — the HTTP REST API for telescope control — are available for C#. Second, WPF provides the data-binding, template system, and dark-theme support needed for an observatory application. Third, .NET Framework 4.8 is included with current Windows 10 and Windows 11 releases, so end users do not need to install a separate runtime.
body.p_5: The MCP server runs on .NET 8 — a separate project, compiled independently, because the server needs modern .NET features (minimal APIs, source generators) that .NET Framework 4.8 does not support. The two .NET runtimes coexist cleanly: the main app spawns the MCP server as a child process and communicates via HTTP.
body.p_6: Python handles two subsystems whose main libraries are Python-native: voice recognition and certain image processing scripts. The voice pipeline uses faster-whisper (SYSTRAN's CTranslate2 port of OpenAI's Whisper) for speech-to-text, Silero VAD for voice activity detection, and gTTS or edge-tts for text-to-speech feedback. These libraries depend on PyTorch and CTranslate2, which have no maintained C# bindings of comparable maturity.
body.p_7: The post-processing scripts use numpy for AI denoising (a-trous wavelet transforms), star removal (morphological opening), and super-resolution (bicubic upscale + unsharp mask). These were reimplemented from scratch in numpy because the original Seti Astro Suite Pro scripts were reference implementations, not redistributable code. The numpy implementations are dependency-light — they run on any machine with Python and numpy, no GPU required.
body.p_8: Python is bundled in the installer as an embeddable CPython 3.11 distribution (~1.4 GB) with all pip packages pre-installed. The main C# application launches Python scripts as subprocesses, communicates via stdout/stdin JSON, and manages their lifecycle. Because Python runs in separate processes, Python version conflicts and DLL clashes are kept out of the main application.
body.p_9: The C++ layer also wraps the Canon EDSDK for direct live view integration with Canon DSLRs — a P/Invoke bridge to Canon's proprietary native DLL. This bypasses the ASCOM still-exposure workaround and provides real-time electronic viewfinder on supported bodies.
body.p_10: The embedded web dashboard is a single-file HTML application served by the C# web server on port 8090. It uses no framework — vanilla JavaScript with CSS Grid and WebSocket for real-time updates. The choice was deliberate: a framework would add build complexity, bundle size, and dependency risk for a dashboard that needs to work reliably in the field on any device.
body.p_11: The dashboard includes a live status panel, image preview with zoom/pan/histogram, remote joystick control for the mount, filter wheel and cooler controls, real-time Kalman filter charts (RA/Dec error, confidence, covariance trace), a scheduler with mosaic wizard, and a live log viewer. It supports PWA installation on phone and tablet home screens, and includes a night-vision mode that turns the UI red to preserve dark adaptation.
body.p_12: Every language boundary is a process boundary or a network boundary. No in-process DLL conflicts. No runtime version collisions. Python exceptions don't propagate to the C# app.
body.p_13: Python is embedded in the installer. The user installs one EXE and gets everything. No "install Python 3.11, then pip install these 20 packages" instructions.
body.p_14: C# for WPF and ASCOM. Python for Whisper and numpy. C++ for native math. HTML for the web dashboard. Each language is used where its libraries or platform support are needed.
body.p_15: 347+ unit tests run without hardware. The Kalman filter can be tested without a mount. The voice parser can be tested without a microphone. The web dashboard can be tested without a telescope.
body.p_26: The C++ layer is small but performance-critical. Two projects — HybridTelescopeControl.Core and HybridTelescopeControl.Shared — provide native astro math utilities called via P/Invoke from C#. These include coordinate transformations, matrix operations, and numerical routines that benefit from native compilation.
body.p_27: 7 tabs: Dashboard, Image Preview, Remote Control, Tracking, Mount Model, Scheduler, Logs
body.p_31: The build and packaging pipeline uses three scripting languages. BUILD.bat orchestrates MSBuild compilation. BUILD_INSTALLER_NSIS.bat runs the NSIS compiler, stages ~4.9 GB of dependencies, compresses with 7z LZMA2, and creates a self-extracting installer. PowerShell scripts handle deployment via SCP/SSH to the production server, installer upload with progress tracking, and license key generation.

article.headline: How HYBRID Compares with NINA, SGP, and APT
article.deck: NINA, SGP, and APT are established tools that each cover a large part of the imaging workflow. HYBRID takes a different approach: an all-in-one, voice-first control system with AI orchestration. This article lists where the feature sets overlap and where they differ.

sidebar.stat_desc: Features built into HYBRID that the other applications in this comparison do not include out of the box. Some are available elsewhere through plugins or companion tools.

sections.tracking_title: 3. Predictive Tracking — Kalman, EKF, and ML

body.h2_4: 3. Predictive Tracking — Kalman, EKF, and ML
body.p_1: NINA (Nighttime Imaging 'N' Astronomy) is a free, open-source application for imaging and sequencing. Sequence Generator Pro (SGP) is a commercial application for automated acquisition. APT (Astro Photography Tool) is a commercial acquisition tool that many beginners start with. All three are mature and actively maintained.
body.p_2: HYBRID Telescope Control is not designed to replace these tools at what they do. Its focus is different: it combines voice control, AI orchestration, predictive tracking, image processing, and remote observatory management in one application, with spoken or typed commands as the primary interaction. The comparison below covers built-in features as understood at the time of writing. NINA in particular extends its functionality through plugins, and the other applications may offer some capabilities through companion software.
body.p_3: Voice control is HYBRID's central feature. A spoken command such as "slew to M31, plate solve, and start imaging for 90 minutes" is translated into the corresponding mount, solver, and camera actions. Three voice backends handle the same commands: Claude Desktop via MCP for cloud AI reasoning, local llama.cpp for fully offline operation, and a built-in Whisper grammar parser as a zero-dependency fallback. The other applications in this comparison do not include a built-in voice interface.
body.p_4: The voice system has its own error handling, spoken feedback, and safety mechanisms rather than only forwarding commands to existing functions. The parser handles 210+ natural language phrase variants across 55 distinct actions. Context-aware stop commands stop tracking, video, slew, or scheduler depending on what is running. Emergency stop is always available.
body.p_5: NINA, SGP, and APT typically delegate guiding to PHD2, which measures guide-star error and sends corrections — a feedback approach. HYBRID adds a 3-layer predictive tracking model: passive sidereal (Layer 1), active Kalman/EKF feedback (Layer 2), and ML-enhanced noise tuning (Layer 3). The Kalman filter estimates the mount's drift and applies corrections based on that estimate, ahead of the next measurement.
body.p_6: Guide star → measure error → send pulse guide correction. Corrects after the error occurs. Latency: 1-3 seconds.
body.p_7: Plate solve → Kalman filter predicts drift → apply correction from the prediction. ML learns periodic error patterns. Corrections do not wait for the next guide frame; their accuracy depends on the quality of the drift model.
body.p_8: NINA focuses on acquisition, PixInsight on post-processing, and PHD2 on guiding. HYBRID covers parts of all three in one application: mount control, camera control, image stacking, calibration, plate solving, scheduling, weather, annotation, and remote web access. The trade-off is depth — NINA's sequencer is more capable and PixInsight's processing more sophisticated. The difference is that in HYBRID these functions share one application and one command interface.
body.p_9: The ngrok-based tunnel with JWT session authentication lets you control the observatory from any device over the internet. No VPN, no port forwarding, no firewall configuration. The 7-tab web dashboard includes live status, image preview with zoom/pan/histogram, remote joystick control, filter wheel and cooler controls, real-time Kalman charts, and a scheduler. PWA support means you can install it on your phone's home screen.
body.p_10: When the WPF UI thread freezes — a rare but possible event during long ASCOM calls or Python subprocess hangs — a background watchdog thread detects the freeze and auto-restarts the application. Session state is recovered from the last 30-second auto-save. The feature is intended for unattended imaging rigs; the other applications in this comparison do not document an equivalent built-in watchdog.
body.p_11: One-click buttons for AI Denoise (a-trous wavelet transforms), Star Removal (morphological opening), and Super-Resolution (bicubic upscale + unsharp mask). When Seti Astro Cosmic Clarity is installed, HYBRID uses its trained PyTorch models. Otherwise, the built-in numpy implementations run on CPU. The acquisition applications in this comparison leave post-processing to separate software.
body.p_12: Nine rejection algorithms for image stacking — from standard sigma-clipping to Linear Fit Clipping and Generalized ESD. GPU-accelerated via ILGPU. SPCC color calibration. Drizzle CFA and mosaic stacking. These are features users typically open Siril or PixInsight for.
body.p_13: NINA's Advanced Sequencer is more powerful and flexible for complex multi-target imaging plans. HYBRID's scheduler is simpler but less configurable.
body.p_14: SGP has years of production use. HYBRID is newer; its code audit found edge cases that more mature software has typically already addressed.
body.p_15: PHD2 is a dedicated guiding application with years of field use across many mounts. HYBRID's built-in tracking is newer and has been tested on a smaller range of equipment.
body.p_16: PixInsight's post-processing is far more extensive. HYBRID's built-in tools are intended for quick previews, not final processing.
body.p_17: The Model Context Protocol gives any MCP-compatible AI assistant access to 47 telescope tools. Claude Desktop can chain tools: "goto M81, plate solve, autofocus, and start imaging for 30 minutes with 180-second exposures" becomes a sequence of goto_target, plate_solve, autofocus, start_imaging calls. At the time of writing, an MCP server is not a built-in feature of the other applications compared here.

article.headline: The Inspiration Map — Where HYBRID's Ideas Came From
article.deck: HYBRID Telescope Control draws on more than 20 existing projects — from NINA's sequencer to Anthropic's Model Context Protocol, from Siril's stacking to Seti Astro's AI post-processing. This map lists what was adopted from each.

sidebar.stat_desc: Telescope control software, AI tools, voice recognition, image processing, and web frameworks that influenced HYBRID's design.

body.p_1: HYBRID builds on work done by other projects. NINA, SGP, and PHD2 had already solved problems that were studied before HYBRID's design was settled. The Model Context Protocol provides the standard that HYBRID's AI-driven telescope control uses. faster-whisper and Silero VAD form the voice recognition stack that the voice pipeline depends on. This article lists where each idea came from, what was adopted, and what was developed specifically for HYBRID.
body.p_2: A free, open-source telescope sequencing application. HYBRID adopted the concept of equipment profiles (save/load telescope+camera+filter configs) and the sequencer's target-based workflow. NINA's plugin architecture showed that a telescope app could be extensible without being monolithic.
body.p_3: A commercial acquisition application known for its session handling. HYBRID's session management (auto-save every 30 seconds, crash recovery) was modeled on SGP's state persistence. SGP's meridian flip logic was studied for the pier-side verification approach.
body.p_4: A widely used dedicated autoguiding application. HYBRID integrates with PHD2 for dither settle and guide-star-lost detection, and also includes its own Kalman-based tracking as an alternative. PHD2's approach to guide star selection and dither patterns influenced HYBRID's tracking design.
body.p_5: HYBRID embeds the Stellarium Web Engine (WASM, BSD 3-Clause) as its in-app sky chart. The real-time sky view, DSS deep-sky overlay, and reticle tracking are all Stellarium technology. The sky chart is HYBRID's most visible borrowed component.
body.p_6: The ASCOM Platform is the standard hardware interface for telescope control on Windows. HYBRID's ASCOMControllerWrapper is an Alpaca HTTP REST client covering mount, camera, focuser, rotator, filter wheel, dome, switch, and safety monitor. Because of ASCOM, HYBRID does not need a custom driver for each mount vendor.
body.p_7: Han Kleijn's ASTAP is HYBRID's primary local plate solver. It runs offline and solves quickly. HYBRID also supports Astrometry.net for cloud solving. ASTAP's hinted-solve mode (using the mount's approximate position) was adopted for speed.
body.p_8: The Model Context Protocol is Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools. HYBRID's 47 MCP tools follow this standard. Claude Desktop is the primary voice backend — it interprets telescope commands and chains MCP tool calls.
body.p_9: The CTranslate2 port of OpenAI's Whisper model. HYBRID uses the small.en variant for near-real-time transcription. Silero VAD (from the same ecosystem) handles voice activity detection. Together they form the core of HYBRID's voice input pipeline.
body.p_10: The local LLM backends that make fully offline voice control possible. HYBRID's llama.cpp bridge connects to a local Qwen3 model for remote observatories without internet. Ollama provides a simpler alternative for users who prefer its model management.
body.p_11: HYBRID includes a voice bridge for VS Code Copilot Chat, allowing developers to control the telescope from their editor. The bridge was modeled after Claude Desktop's MCP integration but adapted for Copilot's different protocol.
body.p_12: The free, open-source astro image processor. HYBRID's stacking algorithms (sigma-clipping, Winsorized, median) were validated against Siril's output. Siril's background extraction (RBF thin-plate spline + polynomial) was studied for HYBRID's BackgroundExtractionEngine. Siril 1.4.2 source was included in build staging for reference.
body.p_13: The professional standard for astro image processing. HYBRID's SPCC color calibration and drizzle algorithms reference PixInsight's approach. HYBRID's post-processing is positioned as a preview tool — users are expected to take HYBRID's linear masters into PixInsight for final production.
body.p_14: The original source of the AI Denoise, Star Removal, and Super-Resolution algorithms. HYBRID's numpy implementations were reimplemented from scratch based on SASpro's reference scripts. When Seti Astro Cosmic Clarity (trained PyTorch models) is installed, HYBRID uses those instead.
body.p_15: SharpCap's live-stacking behavior (Winsorized rejection, automatic background neutralization) was used as a reference for HYBRID's stacking engine. The dev log explicitly notes that HYBRID's winsorize behavior "matches SharpCap."
body.p_16: Three features have no direct counterpart in the telescope software reviewed for this project. First, conversational voice control with AI orchestration. The voice pipeline (microphone → VAD → STT → parser → MCP dispatch → ASCOM command) was designed specifically for HYBRID, because the existing voice integrations for hardware control that were reviewed did not handle astronomical commands.
body.p_17: Second, the 3-layer predictive tracking model (sidereal + Kalman/EKF + ML). PHD2's guiding works by feedback: it measures the error, then corrects it. HYBRID's tracking is predictive — it uses a Kalman filter to estimate the mount's drift state and applies corrections based on that estimate. The ML layer learns periodic error patterns over time. The approach is common in aerospace and robotics and less common in amateur astronomy software.
body.p_18: Third, the UI-freeze watchdog with auto-restart and session recovery is a reliability feature borrowed from industrial control systems rather than telescope software. A background thread monitors the UI thread's responsiveness; if it freezes beyond a configurable threshold (default 45 seconds), the watchdog kills and restarts the application, recovering state from the last auto-save. It is intended for unattended imaging rigs running for 6+ hours.
body.p_19: Primary IDE. MSBuild Release|x64 via BUILD.bat. SDK-style .csproj with auto-include. C# 7.3 language version.
body.p_20: Installer pipeline: NSIS compile → stage ~4.9 GB → 7z LZMA2 → SFX. Output: single ~2.64 GB EXE.
body.p_21: 347+ unit tests across GUI (161), ImageProcessing (357), Camera (34), and WebUI (25 Playwright). Hardware-independent regression tests.
body.p_22: Website build (Vite + TypeScript). Server-side analytics (server_with_analytics.cjs). Deployed via SCP/SSH.

article.headline: The 48 Features — A Complete Catalog
article.deck: From plate solving to dome automation, from voice control to PEC analysis — every capability of the voice-controlled observatory, cataloged and explained.

sidebar.stat_desc: Organized across 8 categories: Tracking, Voice, Imaging, Session, System, Processing, Remote, and Integration.

body.p_1: HYBRID Telescope Control combines mount tracking with voice input, plate solving, automatic error correction, and control of the other observatory subsystems from a single laptop. This catalog documents its forty-eight discrete features, from Kalman-filter predictive tracking to voice commands in two languages.
body.p_2: The standard HYBRID package ships with 41 features covering tracking, imaging, automation, and system management. The Pro tier adds seven capabilities that extend HYBRID from telescope control to observatory equipment such as domes, power switches, and flat panels. Each one interfaces with an external hardware protocol and has its own state management.
body.p_3: INDI and Alpaca dome protocol support. The dome shutter, rotation, and home index are tracked in real time. Park, track, and wire modes allow the dome to follow the mount through meridian flips and target switches without manual intervention. Auto sync keeps the dome slit aligned with the telescope's optical axis during the session.
body.p_4: Four-channel relay management with per-switch naming, auto-off timers, and a live power budget display. Each switch can be assigned to a subsystem — mount, camera, dew heater, focuser — and configured with independent on/off schedules. The power budget tracker prevents overloads by monitoring total draw against supply capacity.
body.p_5: Absolute positioning with backlash compensation in both directions. Auto focus routines use HFR (half-flux radius) measurement to find the critical focus zone. Filter offsets allow refocusing when switching between narrowband and broadband filters without repeating the full autofocus cycle.
body.p_6: Angle synchronization keeps the camera oriented correctly relative to the target throughout long exposures. Meridian flip rotation compensates for the 180-degree image rotation that occurs during pier-side transitions. Framing presets store preferred position angles for common targets.
body.p_7: Flat panel control for calibration frames. The system manages panel brightness, exposure duration, and session planning for dusk/dawn flats. Integration with the sequence engine allows automated flat frames at session start or end.
body.p_8: A plate-solve-based routine modeled on the TVC (Takahashi Variation Correction) method. It targets a polar alignment accuracy of plus or minus 5 arcseconds through iterative star measurements and mount offset calculations. No additional hardware is required beyond the main imaging camera.
body.p_9: A single command that frames a target by centering it in the field and rotating the camera to the desired position angle. The system plate-solves, calculates the offset, slews the mount, and rotates the camera in sequence — all without user intervention.
body.p_10: The tracking stack underpins the other features: image quality and automation both depend on accurate tracking. HYBRID implements twelve distinct tracking subsystems that work together.
body.p_11: A 4×4 state-space model tracking RA position, RA velocity, Dec position, and Dec velocity. The filter fuses mount encoder readings with plate-solve corrections to produce a predicted state that smooths out periodic error, backlash, and atmospheric refraction artifacts. An extended Kalman filter variant handles nonlinear Jacobian matrices when tracking rates deviate significantly from sidereal.
body.p_12: Direct integration with OnStepX via serial and network connections. INDI drivers provide an abstraction layer for mounts, cameras, and accessories. Both paths are supported simultaneously — a user can run OnStepX on a Raspberry Pi while the Windows laptop handles image processing and scheduling.
body.p_13: Standard ASCOM PulseGuide interface with 100-millisecond pulse resolution on both RA and Dec axes. Compatible with PHD2, MetaGuide, and any other guiding application that speaks ASCOM.
body.p_14: Over 3,000 objects with magnitude, seasonal visibility, and current altitude data. The catalog is queried in real time to suggest targets based on observability windows, moon illumination, and user preferences.
body.p_15: Powered by astrometry.net, the plate solver can recover pointing without a position hint, including when the mount's position is unknown. Solve times range from 2 seconds for well-exposed star fields to 30 seconds for faint-field solutions.
body.p_16: A 5-second cadence plate-solve loop that continuously syncs the mount's reported position with the actual sky coordinates. The feedback is fed back into the Kalman filter, creating a closed-loop tracking system that corrects drift in real time.
body.p_17: FFT analysis of tracking errors reveals the worm gear's periodic signature. HYBRID captures the error waveform, fits a correction curve, and exports it directly to OnStepX for hardware-level PEC playback. The aim is sub-arcsecond tracking without autoguiding; the achieved result depends on the mount and the seeing.
body.p_18: HYBRID ships voice control as a working production feature rather than a demo. It handles 210+ phrase variants across 55+ actions in French and English, with support for ten or more dialects.
body.p_19: OpenAI Whisper large-v3 runs locally on the GPU for sub-second transcription. A Silero VAD (voice activity detection) combined with an energy gate provides dual-layer noise filtering that rejects wind, traffic, and dew heater hum without clipping speech.
body.p_20: Every major subsystem is voice-controllable: slew to target, start imaging, run autofocus, check weather, park the mount, open the dome. Commands are parsed with fuzzy matching — "point at Andromeda" and "slew to M31" both resolve to the same target.
body.p_21: Local processing for low-latency control. Gemini CLI for conversational target selection and session planning. Claude CLI for complex multi-step commands and natural language scripting. Users can switch backends mid-session based on connectivity and complexity.
body.p_22: 47 tools exposed via Model Context Protocol with OpenAI function calling format. Any LLM that supports function calling can control the telescope — not just the built-in backends.
body.p_23: FITS image processing is a core part of HYBRID. Fifteen distinct analysis methods cover everything from basic statistics to star shape characterization.
body.p_24: HFR-based filtering with quality grades A through D. Frames exceeding the user-defined FWHM or eccentricity thresholds are automatically rejected before stacking. This removes frames with trailing, bloated stars, or clouds without manual inspection.
body.p_25: Automatic background modeling using mesh interpolation. The extracted background is subtracted from each frame, removing gradient artifacts from light pollution, moon glow, and vignetting.
body.p_26: Three stacking algorithms: median for maximum outlier rejection, mean for best signal-to-noise, and sigma-clipped mean for a balance of both. Stacks update in real time as new frames arrive, producing a progressively deeper image throughout the session.
body.p_27: 8-bit preview images exported as PNG, JPEG, or TIFF for quick sharing. The full 16-bit or 32-bit FITS data is preserved separately for scientific processing.
body.p_28: An observatory session is a sequence of decisions, adjustments, and contingencies that unfold over hours. HYBRID automates the main steps of that workflow.
body.p_29: Targets are queued with altitude constraints, moon avoidance windows, and priority scores. The scheduler reorders the queue in real time as conditions change — a target rising above the horizon takes precedence over one sinking behind trees.
body.p_30: When the mount approaches the meridian, HYBRID pauses imaging, verifies pier side, flips the mount, re-centers the target, and resumes — without user intervention. The plate-solve feedback loop is designed to re-acquire the target within 2 arcseconds of its pre-flip position.
body.p_31: PHD2 integration via ASCOM. Dithering between frames reduces walking noise patterns. Guiding calibration is automated at session start, and guide star selection uses the same HFR metrics as the main imaging pipeline.
body.p_32: N-step sequences with loops, conditional logic, and sub-frame selection. A typical sequence might be: 20×300s L, 15×300s R, 15×300s G, 15×300s B, each with autofocus triggers every 10 frames and flat calibration between filter changes.
body.p_33: Weather data from OpenWeatherMap and Meteoblue is polled continuously. Wind speed, cloud cover, and humidity thresholds trigger automatic session abort. The safety monitor is independent of the main control loop — it cannot be overridden by voice commands or automation scripts.
body.p_34: The remaining eight features in the core package address system reliability, remote access, and integration with the broader home automation ecosystem.
body.p_35: A background monitor that detects application freezes and triggers automatic restart. The watchdog preserves session state across restarts, so the session resumes from the last auto-save after a UI crash.
body.p_36: Multi-machine architecture allows remote monitoring from any device with a web browser. The laptop next to the mount handles hardware communication; a desktop across the house provides the control interface. Both stay synchronized via WebSocket state replication.
body.p_37: Real-time status display — mount position, camera state, weather, guiding error, stacking progress — served from the local machine. No installation required on the viewing device. Works on phones, tablets, and laptops.
body.p_38: Every session is recorded: target coordinates, exposure times, guiding metrics, weather conditions, and user actions. The database is fully searchable, enabling historical analysis of tracking performance across months of data.
body.p_39: Observatory state is published to an MQTT broker for home automation integration. Node-RED, Home Assistant, and custom scripts can subscribe to mount position, session status, and safety alerts.
body.p_40: Over 60 endpoints expose the main subsystems. The API is documented, versioned, and supports both JSON and message-pack serialization. Custom frontends, mobile apps, and third-party tools can control the observatory without using the HYBRID UI.
body.p_41: The final four features target users who operate multi-equipment setups and need structured configuration and data management.
body.p_42: Saved configurations for telescope, camera, mount, and filter wheel combinations. Switching between a wide-field refractor setup and a deep-sky SCT rig takes one click instead of reconfiguring every parameter manually.
body.p_43: Two weather data sources — OpenWeatherMap for general conditions and Meteoblue for astronomical seeing forecasts. Both are polled at configurable intervals, and the data feeds directly into the safety monitor and scheduler.
body.p_44: The daemon, web, and desktop components can run on separate machines. The daemon handles hardware communication on the mount-side laptop. The web dashboard runs on any device. The desktop app provides the full Electron interface on a control room machine. State synchronization between them is automatic.
body.p_45: Full session data export in JSON format. Import previous sessions for comparison, reproduce imaging runs, or transfer configurations to a new machine. The export includes target metadata, exposure sequences, guiding logs, and weather records.
